prompt: Write an essay arguing whether schools should start later in the morning.
text:
# Schools Should Start Later

Most teenagers are tired in the morning, and it is not because they are lazy. Puberty shifts the body's internal clock, so adolescents tend to get sleepy later at night and wake later in the morning. A 15-year-old who is asked to be alert at 7:30 a.m. is working against biology. Schools should start later, and the evidence for the change is stronger than the objections to it.

## The sleep problem

Medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, recommend that teenagers sleep eight to ten hours a night. Most do not. When first period begins at 7:30 or earlier, a student who falls asleep at 11 p.m. has to wake around 6 a.m. to get ready and commute. That leaves seven hours at best. Many students lose more, because homework, jobs and activities push bedtime later still.

Going to bed earlier is the obvious reply, but it ignores the clock shift. A teenager cannot simply decide to feel sleepy at 9 p.m. Telling students to sleep more while the schedule makes it impossible puts the blame on the wrong party.

## What the research shows

Districts that moved their start times later have been studied for years. Students in these districts generally sleep longer, and they report less daytime drowsiness and fewer symptoms of depression. Some studies find higher attendance and fewer tardies. Several also find fewer car crashes among teen drivers, which makes sense, since drowsy driving is a leading danger for that age group. Results on grades and test scores are more mixed, but the direction is usually positive or neutral, and I know of no strong evidence that later starts hurt achievement.

## The objections

The strongest objections are practical, not scientific.

**Buses and budgets.** Many districts run one set of buses in tiers: high school first, then middle, then elementary. Moving the high school later forces a rearrangement, and that can cost money. Still, some districts have managed it by adjusting routes or swapping the order of the tiers. The cost is real, but so is the cost of a generation that is chronically short on sleep.

**Sports and jobs.** Later dismissal can cut into practice time, and it can conflict with after-school work. These are scheduling problems, and schools can address them with adjusted practice times or shared facilities. They are not reasons to keep a schedule that harms students' health.

**Family routines.** Parents who leave for work early may worry about who supervises teens or younger siblings in the morning. That concern deserves attention, but a later start gives teenagers more time at home, not less, and families have adapted when districts have made the change.

## Conclusion

A school schedule is a choice, not a law of nature. Early start times were set around buses, budgets and adult work hours, not around what helps students learn. When a different schedule offers more sleep, better health and safer roads for a modest administrative cost, the case for keeping the old one is weak. Districts should move high school start times to 8:30 a.m. or later and plan around the logistical problems instead of letting them decide the question.
